title: "4 - Variability, sampling variability and uncertainty"

<div class="intro-chapter"><p class="intro">Chapter 2 explored variability as a property of environmental systems: conditions differ across places and through time, organisms differ from one another, and ecological processes can produce a wide range of outcomes even under superficially similar conditions. Chapter 3 added the observation process, showing how our measurements represent aspects of that system with varying completeness and accuracy. We now need to consider what happens when we try to learn about a variable population from a limited number of observations. We can rarely measure every tree, site, place or moment relevant to our question. Instead, we sample a subset and use what we find to estimate something about the whole. Another subset would normally give a somewhat different answer, even if our measurements were perfect and nothing in the population had changed. We will first make that problem visible by imagining a small forest landscape whose full biomass distribution is known, then return to the more realistic situation where only one sample is available. The aim is to understand how population variability, sample size and sampling design influence uncertainty, before considering how that reasoning extends to comparisons, relationships and nested ecological data.</p></div>
:::

## 4.1 · Why different samples of the same population give different estimates {#ch4-s41}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>Imagine a small forest landscape divided into 100 equal-area plots. For this exercise only, suppose we know the aboveground biomass of every plot. Some plots contain relatively little biomass while others contain much more; together, these 100 values describe our population. We can calculate its actual mean and see how strongly biomass varies across the landscape. In field research we rarely know the full population, but this artificial situation allows us to examine what our estimates would do if we pretended to know only the plots selected by a sampling procedure. Select five different plots at random, calculate their mean and put them back into the pool of plots that could be sampled in the next exercise. Select another five and calculate a second mean. We will generally obtain different values, although both samples came from exactly the same landscape and were selected in exactly the same way. One may happen to include several high-biomass patches and the other more low-biomass patches. This difference among possible estimates is <strong>sampling variability</strong>. The variation in biomass among the 100 plots, which was already present before we selected anything, is <strong>ecological variability</strong>. The distinction is about what varies: the actual population units in one case, and the estimates from alternative samples in the other.</p>
<p>To see what adding observations does, start with a single plot and calculate its biomass as our provisional estimate of the population mean. Add a second plot and calculate their mean, then a third, and continue to twenty. Early in the sequence, the addition of an unusually high or low value may move the estimate substantially. Once many plots contribute to the average, one more observation usually has a smaller influence. The running mean illustrates how one estimate evolves while a sample accumulates; it does not imply that the true landscape becomes less variable as we measure more plots. We can use this intuition to make a more systematic comparison. Instead of extending one sample, imagine collecting many complete samples of exactly five plots, calculating a mean for each and plotting all those means. This is the <em>sampling distribution</em> of the five-plot mean for our chosen procedure. Repeat the exercise with samples of twenty plots. The twenty-plot means usually cluster more closely around the true landscape mean, even though individual plots retain precisely the same spread of biomass values. A particular twenty-plot sample can still produce an unusually high or low mean; the important pattern becomes visible across the many possible samples.</p>

<figcaption><span class="figure-label">Figure 4.1.</span> Simulated example based on one fixed population of 100 forest plots. The left panel shows the variation among plot biomass values. On the right, each value represents the mean of one independently repeated sample, drawn without replacement within the sample; the narrower distribution for twenty-plot samples indicates less sampling variability. The dashed line is the true population mean. The population has not changed between the sampling exercises.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Now consider a second landscape with the same mean biomass but much stronger variation among its plots. A small sample from this landscape would be more sensitive to which plots happened to be selected, producing a wider distribution of possible means. Alternatively, if all 100 plots were identical, every sample would have the same mean and sampling variability would disappear for this particular estimator. The two thought experiments reveal why the uncertainty in an estimate depends both on how variable the relevant population units are and on how many of them enter the sample. In the field we normally cannot produce the full sampling distribution because we cannot collect thousands of alternative samples. We must estimate its spread using information from the one sample we actually collected.</p>
<details class="technical"><summary>Worked example 4A · One small sample, two different questions</summary><p>Suppose five plots have biomass values of 40, 60, 70, 220 and 250 Mg ha⁻¹. Their mean is 128 Mg ha⁻¹. Looking at the individual values tells us that biomass varies strongly among these five plots. It does <em>not</em> directly tell us how much the mean would vary if we selected a different five from the larger landscape. To answer the second question we need to connect the observed plot-to-plot variation with the sampling procedure and the number of plots included.</p></details>
</section>
:::

## 4.2 · Using one observed sample to estimate sampling uncertainty {#ch4-s42}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>Return to our forest study, but now assume that only the five sampled plots are known. We can calculate their mean, but the many alternative sample means that made Figure 4.1 possible are hidden from us. We would like to know how stable the estimated mean would be if we could repeat the same sampling procedure. To work towards that answer, we begin with the spread of biomass values among the plots we did measure. The <strong>standard deviation</strong>, usually abbreviated SD, describes how dispersed those individual values are around their sample mean. The usual calculation squares the deviations from the mean, averages them with an adjustment for sample size, and takes the square root. We do not need to work through that algebra here to understand its role: the SD from our sampled plots is information about the heterogeneity of the larger population. Because those five plots are only a subset, their SD may itself be unusually low or high; a different five plots would generally provide a different SD as well as a different mean. We now use that estimated population variability to infer how widely sample means would be distributed if the procedure were repeated. The resulting quantity is the <strong>standard error</strong>, or SE, of our estimated mean. For a simple mean calculated from n appropriately selected, approximately independent units, a familiar approximation is:</p><div class="eq"><strong>SE = SD / √n</strong></div>
<p>Here the SD describes variation among the observed units, while the SE describes the estimated variation among means obtained from alternative samples of the same size. They are not alternative labels for the same spread. There are two ideas in the formula worth considering separately. First, if sample size stays the same, more heterogeneous population units produce more variable sample means; the estimated SE becomes larger when the SD is larger. Second, if the underlying population variability stays the same, including more units in the average generally reduces the SE. The square root makes this decline slower than a simple one-for-one relation: with an SD of 40, sampling four units gives an SE of 20, sixteen units gives an SE of 10, and sixty-four units gives an SE of 5. To halve the SE we need approximately four times as many independent units, not merely twice as many. Sampling provides diminishing gains in precision as n increases, although how much another observation helps in practice also depends on which part of the population it represents.</p>
<details class="technical"><summary>Technical box 4B · Calculate SD and SE for five plots</summary><p>For plot biomass values 40, 60, 70, 220 and 250 Mg ha⁻¹, the mean is 128. The sum of squared deviations from this mean is 39,080. The sample SD is √(39,080 / 4) ≈ 98.84 Mg ha⁻¹. Under the simple independent-unit approximation, the estimated SE is 98.84 / √5 ≈ <strong>44.20 Mg ha⁻¹</strong>. The SD describes spread among the measured plots; the SE is our estimate of how strongly a five-plot mean would vary across repeated samples under the assumed procedure. Both have the same units as biomass.</p><p>For simple random sampling <em>without replacement</em> from a small, finite population, the exact design-based SE also includes a finite-population correction. The familiar SD/√n expression is commonly adequate when the sampling fraction is small; the main chapter uses it to develop the intuition.</p></details>
<p>The inferential step is less secure when our sample is very small. The five plots may by chance include an unusual concentration of high values or miss a major habitat type, so both the mean and our estimate of its precision may be unreliable. This is a second layer of uncertainty that is easy to overlook: we do not know the population mean because we observed only a sample, and we also estimate how uncertain that mean is from the variation found within that same limited sample. Collecting more relevant units tends to improve both estimates. It does not guarantee a good result if the design samples only part of the intended landscape, a problem we will develop after considering how uncertainty appears when we compare groups and fit relationships.</p>
<details class="technical"><summary>Optional sampling exercise · Watch both estimates vary</summary><p>From the imaginary known landscape, draw a five-plot sample and calculate its mean, SD and SE. Replace it with another complete five-plot sample, then repeat several times. The mean varies, but so do the calculated SD and SE. Repeat with n = 10 and n = 20. This makes visible why the uncertainty calculated from a single sample is itself an estimate, not a known property of that sample's mean. Later, when we no longer know the full population, bootstrap resampling will offer one approximate route to exploring the same idea.</p></details>
</section>
:::

## 4.3 · Estimating ecological differences and relationships {#ch4-s43}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>Suppose our question is no longer the mean biomass of one landscape but whether two land uses differ in soil infiltration. We select independent sampling areas within each land use and calculate the difference between their sample means. If infiltration varies little among comparable areas, a modest sample may give a fairly stable estimate of the difference. If the areas within each land use are highly heterogeneous, another set of sampled areas could lead to a rather different estimate, even when the true difference between land uses is unchanged. Increasing the number of areas generally stabilises the estimate, but cannot make the underlying landscape more uniform. Consequently, the <em>size of the ecological difference</em>, the <em>variation among the relevant units</em> and our <em>uncertainty about the estimated difference</em> need to be considered together. A striking sample contrast is not automatically well estimated when it is based on few variable units; a modest contrast can be estimated quite precisely when sufficient independent information is available.</p>

<figcaption><span class="figure-label">Figure 4.2.</span> Four illustrative comparisons in which the underlying within-group SD has been held the same. Each panel includes the individual observations, a boxplot, and an orange estimate of the mean ± one SE. We compare large and small mean differences at two sample sizes. A larger sample generally reduces uncertainty around the estimated means without changing the population difference or the variation among population units. Values are constructed for teaching, not field observations.</figcaption></figure>
<p>With a continuous predictor the reasoning is similar but the question changes. Imagine relating biomass to forest age across a series of secondary-forest sites. The fitted regression line estimates a tendency over the observed age range. Individual forests depart from it because age is not the only influence on biomass and because observations are imperfect. A steeper or shallower fitted slope describes the estimated magnitude of the relationship, while the spread of forests around the line and the quantity and placement of observations affect its uncertainty. Twenty forests concentrated near ten years of age cannot characterise a trajectory across ages 1–30 as well as twenty forests distributed across that interval. We therefore need information over the predictor range relevant to the ecological question; adding more forests of nearly the same age does not solve poor coverage of the trajectory.</p>

## 4.4 · Confidence intervals and an approximation from resampling {#ch4-s44}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>When we report an estimated mean or difference, a single number does not show how much it might change if we had selected another comparable sample. The SE expresses this uncertainty as an estimated spread of possible estimates. A <strong>confidence interval</strong> presents it as a range around the observed estimate. One way to understand a 95% confidence procedure is to return to our imaginary landscape: repeatedly select a sample, calculate its mean and draw an interval using the same statistical procedure. Some intervals will include the true population mean and others will miss it. If the procedure works as intended under its assumptions, approximately 95% of those intervals will contain the fixed population mean over many repetitions. In practice we see only the interval from the sample we collected, so we should read it as a statement about the precision of an estimate under the specified sampling and analysis procedure, not as proof that every relevant source of uncertainty has been captured.</p>
<p>For an intuitive picture, consider the familiar approximate interval <strong>mean ± 2 × SE</strong>. This is not a universal confidence-interval formula—small samples and different estimators require appropriate methods—but it shows how an estimate with a larger SE produces a wider interval. For the five-plot example in Box 4B, the SE is approximately 44 Mg ha⁻¹, so a two-SE band would extend about 88 units on either side of the mean of 128. We would not present this as a definitive 95% interval for five plots: the estimated spread is itself unstable when n is small. The exercise nevertheless shows how the earlier repeated-sampling reasoning leads to a visible expression of uncertainty around an estimate. It also helps distinguish an interval around a mean from the full range of individual plot biomass values; the two answer different questions.</p>
<p>What can we do when we want to explore sampling variability but cannot repeatedly collect new field samples? The <strong>bootstrap</strong> constructs many new datasets by resampling our existing observations <em>with replacement</em>, keeping the same sample size, and recalculating the estimate for each resample. A particular plot can therefore appear twice or more in one bootstrap sample and be absent from another. The resulting spread of estimates gives us an approximation to sampling uncertainty using the ecological variation represented in our observed sample. This does not conjure up observations from forest types we never visited. If our field design sampled only dry ridges, a thousand bootstrap samples cannot tell us what the valley forests would have contributed. Similarly, when leaves are nested within trees or plots are nested within sites, resampling should respect the levels that provide independent information; resampling every leaf as though it represented a separate forest would produce misleadingly narrow uncertainty for a forest-level question.</p>
<details class="technical"><summary>Technical box 4C · A short bootstrap worked example</summary><p>Start from biomass values 40, 60, 70, 220 and 250. One possible bootstrap sample of five values is 40, 40, 70, 220, 250; its mean is 124. Another is 60, 70, 70, 220, 220, with mean 128. Repeat this procedure many times and plot the means. This distribution describes what the observed five values imply about possible sample-to-sample variation under bootstrap resampling. It is particularly rough with such a small original sample. An interval calculated from the bootstrap distribution is still conditional on the sample's coverage and on how resampling represents the original design.</p></details>
</section>
:::

## 4.5 · More measurements do not necessarily mean more independent information {#ch4-s45}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>Imagine a dataset containing 32 leaf measurements. That sounds like a sample of 32 observations, but suppose we measured four leaves per tree, two trees per plot, two plots per site, at two forest sites. We then have 32 leaves, eight trees, four plots and only two sites. These numbers are all correct descriptions of the dataset, but they provide different kinds of information. The four leaves on one tree can help us estimate that tree's typical leaf trait and understand variation within its crown; they do not describe four independent trees. The two trees in a plot provide information about variation among trees in one local environment; the two plots within a site tell us something about variation within that site. If our question concerns a site-level difference associated with restoration history, the design contains only two site-level observations. Measuring another hundred leaves on those same trees would not turn them into additional restoration sites.</p>
<p>We can calculate this hierarchy in a simpler worked example. Suppose we measure two leaves on each of two trees in each of two plots. Plot A contains leaf values 10 and 12 on its first tree, and 18 and 20 on its second; the tree means are therefore 11 and 19, giving a plot mean of 15 when the trees contribute equally. In Plot B, tree values 20 and 22, and 26 and 28, give tree means of 21 and 27 and a plot mean of 24. If our target is the difference between the two sampled plots, it is 9 units: the comparison is between plot-level summaries, even though each summary was built from several lower-level measurements. We can obtain a more detailed description of either plot by measuring additional leaves, but generalising the plot contrast to a wider population would require additional appropriately selected plots. If trees contribute different numbers of leaves, we must also decide whether the intended mean gives equal weight to trees or to leaves; averaging all leaf records indiscriminately can answer a different question.</p>
<table><caption>Example 4.1. The same eight leaf measurements summarised at two levels.</caption><thead><tr><th>Plot</th><th>Tree</th><th>Two leaf records</th><th>Tree mean</th><th>Plot mean (equal weight per tree)</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>A</td><td>1</td><td>10, 12</td><td>11</td><td rowspan="2">15</td></tr><tr><td>A</td><td>2</td><td>18, 20</td><td>19</td></tr><tr><td>B</td><td>1</td><td>20, 22</td><td>21</td><td rowspan="2">24</td></tr><tr><td>B</td><td>2</td><td>26, 28</td><td>27</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>In field planning, we may have a choice between adding observations within existing units and selecting further units at a higher level. More leaves can reduce noise around a tree mean; more trees represent tree-to-tree variation; more plots sample distinct local environments; additional sites provide more examples for a site-level comparison. The allocation should follow where variation relevant to the question occurs and at what level we intend to make the inference. There is no universal rule that another subsample is less valuable than another site: when within-tree measurements are very noisy, additional subsamples can initially be worthwhile. The error is to treat every additional measurement as though it expanded the study at every level simultaneously. Chapter 5 develops this distinction between replication and subsampling, including its consequences for feasible sample sizes.</p>
<details class="technical"><summary>Optional design exercise · One more fieldwork day</summary><p>You have already sampled two forest sites, with several plots in each and several soil cores per plot. One day remains. Would you collect more cores from current plots, add plots within current sites or visit a third site? First state the quantity you want to estimate. If it is mean soil carbon in one existing plot, more cores may be informative. If it is variation among plots within a site, new plots offer different information. If it concerns variation among independently selected sites, more cores inside the same sites do not address the principal shortage. Cost and access constrain the decision, but the ecological question should determine what the effort buys.</p></details>
</section>
:::

## 4.6 · What kind of uncertainty is limiting our conclusion? {#ch4-s46}

::: {.env2301-update}
<section><p>We have concentrated on the variability that arises because we observe only a subset of a variable population. Field estimates are also affected by how well we measure the selected units and by the models we use to turn direct measurements into quantities of interest. Consider a study of secondary-forest biomass. We select forest plots, measure the trees in each plot and apply an allometric equation to estimate biomass from tree dimensions and, where available, wood density. If our sample of plots misses important parts of the landscape, our landscape mean may be poorly represented. If diameter measurements are noisy, repeated measurements or better field procedures may help. If an allometric model is inappropriate for the trees being measured, taking more plots cannot by itself fix the conversion from diameter to biomass. We must distinguish these components because additional field effort can reduce one source of uncertainty while leaving others almost untouched.</p>
<p>van Breugel et al. (2011) examined decisions and uncertainties associated with estimating aboveground biomass in tropical secondary forest using field data from 94 plots in central Panama and destructive biomass measurements of 244 trees from 26 locally abundant species. Their results illustrate why the plot-sampling and biomass-modelling components cannot be regarded as one undifferentiated uncertainty. Predictions of stand and landscape biomass varied among allometric models, and the information useful for improving local plot estimates was not necessarily identical to that needed for reducing uncertainty in landscape-level biomass. For our course, the lesson is not to memorise which model performed best in that study. It is to recognise the different stages at which observations are selected, recorded and converted into an estimate. A precise sample average computed from one chosen allometric model is conditional on that modelling decision; an alternative model may produce a different mean from exactly the same inventory.</p>
<p>The same reasoning applies when the main problem is systematic bias rather than model choice. Suppose a sensor regularly reads 5% above the actual value. Averaging more readings may make the result more stable, but it does not remove the 5% offset; calibration addresses a different problem from sample size. Likewise, a large number of roadside plots can precisely characterise roadside conditions while providing poor coverage of a landscape that also contains inaccessible interior forests. We should first ask which part of the study is responsible for the uncertainty that limits our conclusion, then choose what additional information would help: more appropriately distributed independent units, better within-unit measurement, wider spatial or temporal coverage, or a more defensible model or calibration. This brings us naturally to Chapter 5, where sampling decisions are made in relation to the population and comparison we want our observations to represent.</p>
<details class="technical"><summary>Technical box 4D · Precision, error, bias and model uncertainty</summary><p><strong>Ecological variability:</strong> real differences among population units. <strong>Sampling variability:</strong> changes in an estimate that arise because alternative samples contain different units. <strong>Random measurement error:</strong> fluctuations when measuring a unit repeatedly under nominally comparable conditions. <strong>Systematic measurement error or selection bias:</strong> a persistent offset or selection process that favours some values, places or times. <strong>Model uncertainty:</strong> changes in the result arising from uncertain model structure, calibration or parameter values. These categories can interact, and an analysis must specify which are actually quantified by the reported uncertainty interval.</p></details>
</section>
:::
